newsitem.title: ECUADOR: New Ecuador president vows to restore "dignity".
newsitem.headline: New Ecuador president vows to restore "dignity".

text.p: Ecuador's new president Fabian Alarcon has vowed to restore dignity and respect to a country seemingly groggy from the blows of a bizarre political crisis.

Minutes after being sworn in by Congress on Tuesday as interim president, the second time in five days, he said he would introduce a new style in politics based on respect because Ecuadoreans were tired of "insults, bad manners and arrogance."
Alarcon's election for an interim period of 18 months capped a chaotic week in Ecuadorean politics, triggered by the ouster of populist leader Abdala Bucaram.

In Panama, Bucaram slammed Alarcon as "a traitor, a Judas" and said his accession to the presidency was a national disgrace. Bucaram is on a tour of the region to tell Latin American leaders that he was deposed in a disguised coup and to warn "that the same thing could happen to them."

Dismissed by Congress on grounds of "mental incompetence", Bucaram, the self-styled champion of the poor, ruled for only six months with a mixture of eccentricities and boorishness that earned him the nickname of "El loco" (the madman).
"Instability is over, now comes time to work ... we're going to restore dignity to this country ... and respect between government and governed," Alarcon, 49, said.

The vote to appoint him until Aug. 10, 1998 was passed by an overwhelming 57-2 majority in the 82-member Congress, with five abstentions and one blank vote. He is to hand over on Aug. 10, 1998 to a new democratically elected head of state.
General elections are scheduled for early next year and political sources did not rule out an Alarcon candidacy.
In his address to Congress, the new president, a man known for sharp negotiating skills, anticipated a period of belt-tightening measures and asked people to be prepared for sacrifices.

One of his first decrees, he said, would be to repel unpopular measures contained in an austerity package presented by Bucaram last month, including stiff increases in electricity, gas and public transportation rates.
Ecuador's political turmoil, which at one point saw three people claiming the presidency, led some commentators to wonder if Bucaram was the only madman among the country's 12 million people.

A carnival-like confusion saw the defiant Bucaram initially refusing to step down, doing so only when the military withdrew its support. In turn, Vice President Rosalia Arteaga claimed transitional power under what she said were constitutional rules.

What many bemused observers saw as another surreal episode in Latin America's unpredictable politics remained clouded till the end by Arteaga's insistence on respecting the Constitution and not stepping down.

Arteaga, who became Ecuador's first woman president when she took over as head of a caretaker government on Sunday, finally bowed to pressure and left the presidential palace on Tuesday night, returning to her private residence.
But, at a hastily arranged news conference shortly after the start of the congressional session, she called for a referendum within three months to solve the country's "constitutional void."

Embittered by the legislators' refusal to hear her -- the congressional palace's main door remained shut when she showed up -- she said the referendum would ask Ecuadoreans to approve the creation of a constitutional assembly for reforming the State.

Arteaga, a 40-year-old former education minister who was Bucaram's Vice President, said Congress was not constitutionally empowered to appoint presidents. Denouncing petty interests, she lambasted "macho, arrogant" politicians motivated by selfishness.
Some analysts said the political turmoil, which unfolded over carnival holidays, might leave deep scars on the small Andean nation's political scene.

One analyst, who requested anonymity, said Bucaram's swift dismissal could set a dangerous precedent. "Sane leaders could be given the boot for the same crazy reasons ... if the Constitution is not reformed, it will happen again," he said.
